PHANTOM BOTS / ROV OPERATIONSFLL DEMO / QUICK FIRST DIVE

A living world.
In your hands.

Pilot your ROV beneath the surface. Identify zebra and quagga mussels, remove the quagga targets, survey at least 25% of the lake water volume with eDNA samples, and protect the ecosystem. Quaggas start on one side of an invisible invasion front. Use eDNA to investigate that edge. The first level is designed for a 2–3 minute presentation demo, with extra time and budget for practice.

ROV-01 / PILOT GUIDE

You are in control.

Field notes are spoken and shown automatically when you dive in. The next note begins as soon as the previous narration finishes. Use “Voice on” to mute; captions continue. Pausing the game pauses the narration.

Educational fact sources

    ↑ ← ↓ →Aim up, left, down, right
    E / QRise / descend
    SHIFTBoost · $2.80 per meter
    C / X / H / NFire spray / scraper / hydro / eDNA
    1 2 3 4Select tool · Space activates it
    V / ESCChange camera / pause

    Drag the scene to look around. Aim at the small mussels in loose colonies, with a few strays between them. Grouped targets make area tools more effective. The colored ground outline shows your area of effect, and nearby shells have health bars. Native fish, coral, and ribbon grass are wildlife, not targets. Hydro blasting or scraping a fish kills it and costs 2,500 points. Chemicals can also kill fish and other wildlife.

    Chemical spray: $95, 8 m maximum reach, 3.2 m blast radius, 180 damage. Kills good species too: −2,500 points per native fish and −1,500 per aquatic plant. Scores can go negative.
    Scraper: $3, 3 m maximum reach, 1.8 m area. Deals up to 45 damage per pulse, falling to 9 at the limit. Move close and hold Space for repeated pulses.
    Hydro blaster: $40, 6 m maximum reach, 2.6 m area, 120 damage. One-shots mussels within its footprint.
    eDNA monitors possible baby-mussel spread: tiny larvae (veligers) drift through the water before settling. Water tests look for mussel DNA as an early warning; the DNA can come from adults or larvae, so a result alone does not confirm live babies. Sample near and beyond the known infestation. $150 per sample. Each sample represents a 4.5 m radius sphere of water at your current position and depth. Cover at least 25% of the lake’s 3D water volume. Overlapping water counts only once; repeated samples in the same spot add no coverage or points. New water earns up to 90 points per sample. Move between samples, and watch the “next sample” coverage forecast. Amber sampling outlines indicate a local quagga signal; purple outlines indicate no signal detected. Each observation records its position and mission time. Compare sites near the unseen invasion edge, including locations with no detected signal.

    Invasion-front survey: all quaggas start behind a hidden, randomized distribution boundary. This is not a physical wall: the ROV can cross freely, and no line is drawn on the lakebed or sonar. Zebras can occur on rocky beds on either side. Samples report a simplified local quagga-presence signal. Comparing positive and not-detected results helps investigate the edge, but does not prove what caused it or whether quaggas will spread later. This is a fictional research scenario, not a measured Lake Mendota quagga-distribution map. Wisconsin DNR’s documented Lake Mendota record concerns zebra mussels.

    Visual identification: zebra and quagga shells look very similar. Keep a shell visible within 18 m for a total of 3 seconds to identify it. Time accumulates separately for each shell, and looking away does not reset it. Rock and terrain occlusion block identification. The purple strip tracks saved progress; every clearly visible identified shell receives a species-and-distance label. Before identification, no species or distance is displayed. Quaggas earn 5 points and advance the removal goal. Zebras earn zero points and do not advance the goal; they only live on rocky surfaces in this game. Some quaggas also live on rocky patches, so habitat alone does not identify the species. Unknown shells can be removed, but identification helps avoid wasting money.

    The two species use separate shell meshes: a flatter, more angular zebra shell and a rounder, asymmetric quagga shell, with similar coloring. Shell-shape reference: Michigan invasive species guide.

    Each mussel has 100 health. No tool can damage mussels beyond its maximum reach. Level 1 has 240 quaggas in loose colonies and strays, plus 600 more-common zebras attached to rocky bed patches. Remove 80% of the quaggas (192), and sample at least 25% of the lake’s water volume. You get $4,000 and five minutes of practice time; the removal goal is designed to finish in about 2–3 minutes for a presentation. Targets rise by 2.5 percentage points per level, up to 95%, while the lake, population, time, and budget grow.

    Battery: movement costs 0.45% per meter (0.8% boosting), steering uses power, and onboard systems draw a small idle load. Scraper uses 0.25%, hydro 2.5%, chemical 1.7%, and eDNA 1.2% per activation. Surface buoys marked ⚡ on sonar recharge 3% per second (about 33 seconds for a full battery) automatically within 3 m horizontally and above 1.8 m depth. There are two chargers on level 1, with one more added each level. Empty battery or the fifth rock impact triggers an animated explosion and level failure. Pause freezes battery use. Coral blocks movement; steer around its branches.

    Mussel life cycle and fouling: after 20 seconds, surviving breeding mussels begin producing young. Young shells grow to adult size over 36 seconds and then reproduce too, so unchecked populations grow faster. Removing breeders reduces future births. Zebras settle on rocky beds; quaggas stay on their invaded side. New quaggas increase the removal requirement. Spending 6 seconds within 2.3 m of living zebras exposes the ROV to settling young mussels: they attach around the thrusters, reduce thrust, and steadily damage hull health. Moving away stops new attachment, but existing fouling stays. The surface charging station removes fouling at 12% per second; hull damage remains. At zero hull health the ROV explodes. This life cycle is greatly accelerated for gameplay. Real veligers are microscopic drifting larvae, not babies that chase a vehicle; settlement normally takes weeks. Minnesota DNR: zebra mussel life cycle.

    Turning: Left/Right steer normally with a small bank that settles when released. Turning has no runaway limit or full rolls.

    Pitch stability: the up/down arrows tilt the vehicle. Reaching +90° or −90° immediately causes an irreversible runaway, with no recovery window: the ROV spins faster in the tipping direction and accelerates along a fixed path. Steering and tools stop working. The first contact with a rock, coral, lakebed, or lakeshore makes it explode. Stay within the pitch limit or restart after a crash.

    Rock impacts damage the ROV. Five separate collisions destroy it and require a level restart. A sustained push against the same rock counts as one impact; back away before moving again. You can touch the lakebed with Q, and rise with E.

    Ecosystem health: the lake starts stressed by the quagga infestation. Removing quaggas improves its recovery potential. The health bar is calculated from remaining quaggas, the actual living fish and their health, and surviving plants and coral. Dead fish reduce the ecosystem’s ability to recover. Fish become more active as invasive pressure falls. This is a simplified game index, not a scientific prediction of lake recovery.

    All tools have unlimited paid uses. Travel costs $1.70 per meter, or $2.80 with boost. Misses still cost money. Watch the large live score and hull panel in the upper right.

    Sampling spheres and voxel-based water coverage are simplified game rules, not a real eDNA dispersion model or a claim that a bottle physically collects that volume. Treatment effects are also arcade mechanics.
